title: Netanyahu Calls Indian Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar a 'True Hero', Invites Him to Israel
excerpt: In a personal call on October 3, Israel's prime minister invited the hospitalised pilot — and Narendra Modi — to light a flame at Israel's Independence Day ceremony next May.
body:
• Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called Captain Smit Machchhar on October 3, calling the Indian flydubai pilot "a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel."
  • Netanyahu invited Machchhar — and Prime Minister Narendra Modi — to light a flame at Israel's Independence Day national ceremony next May, an honour usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
  • In the call, the hospitalised captain described the cockpit attack: the co-pilot had asked for time to pray, then struck him on the back of the head; "I had that one last fight left in me," he said.
  • UAE investigators have said the co-pilot planned the "terrorist act," attacking Machchhar with an axe aboard the Tel Aviv-bound flight.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday invited the Indian captain of a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight to Israel as a guest of honour, in a personal phone call in which he described the hospitalised pilot as "a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and a hero of the entire world."

"You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world."

— Benjamin Netanyahu, Prime Minister of Israel, to Captain Smit Machchhar

An invitation usually reserved for Israelis

Netanyahu told Captain Smit Machchhar that he wanted both him and Prime Minister Narendra Modi — "one of Israel's key international partners," as The Hindu described him — to light a flame at the national ceremony for Israel's Independence Day next May. The torch-lighting role is traditionally reserved for Israeli citizens, making the invitation a notable diplomatic gesture.

https://x.com/IAjitDoval_IND/status/2106459856328851920

A video of the telephone conversation was released by Netanyahu's office on October 3, the same day the Indian captain gave his first detailed public account of the attack.

The captain's account: "one last fight"

Asked how the attack unfolded, Machchhar said the co-pilot had asked for time to pray, as devout Muslims do five times a day. "A lot of locals, they do pray, which is not out of the ordinary," he said. "While he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back."

Then, after four or five minutes, came a heavy blow to the back of his head. "My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right," Machchhar recalled. "But then after that the blows kept coming one after the other. That's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me."

UAE investigators have said the co-pilot planned the attack as a "terrorist act," using an axe. Machchhar, whose memory he says is not entirely clear because of his injuries, described pulling the cockpit door open once — only for the co-pilot to shut it again — before making a final desperate push.

"I had that one last fight left in me... I pushed against everything. I gave everything that I had and just went for the door and opened the door and thankfully people were waiting."

— Captain Smit Machchhar, flydubai

Context: a hero's welcome at home

Machchhar's story has already made him a celebrated figure in India. Sand artist Sudarsan Pattnaik created a sand sculpture honouring the "hero" captain in Puri, and earlier this week EaseMyTrip announced five years of free domestic flights for him — a gesture reported widely in the Indian press. The Netanyahu invitation elevates the story from national acclaim to an international honour, and draws Modi himself into the commemoration.

What's next

The UAE investigation into the co-pilot's motives continues, and the broader aviation industry will be watching for what investigators conclude about cockpit security on the route. For now, Machchhar remains hospitalised and recovering — with an invitation to light a flame in Jerusalem next May waiting when he is well enough to travel.
